practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of internal (organic) growth?
A) Acquiring a rival company through a takeover
B) Merging with a supplier to reduce costs
C) Launching a new product range funded by retained profit
D) Floating shares on the stock exchange for the first time
practice_questions.marks: C) Launching a new product range funded by retained profit [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline one internal source of finance available to a growing business.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for naming an internal source, plus 1 mark for a linked point that develops it.
• Retained profit (1 mark) — the business reinvests cash it has already earned, so it pays no interest and gives away no ownership (1 mark).
• Also accept: selling assets the business no longer needs.
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one advantage of a business choosing external (inorganic) growth through a takeover.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks: 1 mark for the advantage, plus up to 2 marks for developing it.
• A takeover gives the business immediate access to the other firm's customers, brands and staff (1 mark). This means it can grow far faster than by building those things itself (1 mark), which matters when a rival could reach the same market first (1 mark).
• Also accept: removes a competitor; brings in technology or skilled people the business lacks.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Discuss why a business might choose to become a public limited company (plc) rather than remain a private limited company (Ltd).
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for the two best-developed points only:

Mastering (5-6 marks): Two fully developed points, each with a clear statement and two logical expansion sentences that connect cause to effect for a plc specifically.

Secure (3-4 marks): Two points made, at least one with clear development showing why becoming a plc helps the business achieve its aims.

Developing (1-2 marks): One or two simple points with limited development, such as 'a plc can sell shares to the public'.

Emergent (0 marks): No relevant business knowledge demonstrated.

Content that could be credited:
• Becoming a plc enables the business to raise large amounts of capital through stock market flotation — this provides funds for major investment, acquisitions or expansion into new markets that would be impossible to finance from retained profit or bank loans alone.
• As a plc, the owners benefit from limited liability — shareholders can only lose the amount they invested, making it easier to attract investors who might otherwise be put off by personal financial risk.
• A plc can use its publicly traded shares as currency for acquisitions, offering its own shares rather than cash to buy other businesses, reducing the need for large cash reserves.

practice_questions.text:
Hartwell Engineering Ltd is a precision engineering firm based in the West Midlands with 85 employees and annual revenue of £4.2 million. The owner, Priya Hartwell, has been approached by a German competitor that wants to merge. Priya is also considering pursuing organic growth by investing in new CNC machinery to expand the product range.

Analyse the benefits and drawbacks of Hartwell Engineering Ltd choosing to merge with the German competitor rather than investing in new machinery.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Sustained analysis using specific details from the scenario (Hartwell's 85 staff, £4.2m revenue, precision engineering specialism, West Midlands location) to evaluate the merger versus organic investment. Both benefits and drawbacks are analysed with clear chains of reasoning linked to Hartwell's specific context.

Secure (3–4 marks): Clear analysis of at least two points, with relevant use of context but possibly missing some scenario specifics. Both sides considered but may not be fully balanced.

Developing (2 marks): Some relevant points about mergers or organic growth, but analysis is generic and does not use Hartwell's specific details. Limited exploration of consequences.

Emerging (1 mark): Basic identification of a benefit or drawback with no development or context.

Content that could be credited:
• Merging with the German competitor would give Hartwell immediate access to European markets and a broader customer base, potentially growing revenue far beyond what £4.2m organic growth could achieve — but the culture and language differences could create significant integration challenges for an 85-person firm without a dedicated HR or integration team.
• The merger could bring access to the German company's technology or processes, removing the need to invest in new CNC machinery separately — however, if the German firm's equipment is incompatible, costs could escalate.
• Organic investment preserves Priya's sole control over the direction of the business, whereas a merger would dilute ownership and introduce new decision-makers who may not share her vision for the West Midlands operation.

practice_questions.text:
Cobblestone Candles is a handmade candle brand founded three years ago by Sofia Reyes in Manchester. It currently operates as a sole trader and sells through farmers markets and a small website. Revenue has grown to £180,000 per year. Sofia is considering two options:

Option A: Convert to a private limited company (Ltd) and reinvest profits to launch a national online store.
Option B: Seek a merger with a larger home-fragrance brand to gain immediate national distribution.

Justify which option Sofia should choose.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9 marks): A fully developed recommendation for one option, supported by specific analysis linked to the scenario details (£180,000 revenue, sole trader status, Manchester location, handmade product, online + farmers market channels). Clear evaluative conclusion that acknowledges the rejected option's appeal but explains why the chosen option better suits Cobblestone Candles' context.

Secure (5–7 marks): A clear recommendation with developed analysis of relevant advantages and at least one reason for rejecting the alternative. Uses some scenario context.

Developing (3–4 marks): A preference is stated and some relevant points are made, but the argument is largely generic and could apply to any business rather than Cobblestone Candles specifically.

Emerging (1–2 marks): A basic recommendation with little or no development or context.

Content that could be credited in favour of Option A (Ltd + organic growth):
• Converting to a Ltd protects Sofia's personal assets through limited liability, making further investment less personally risky as the business scales.
• Retaining full ownership means Sofia controls how the brand develops — crucial for a handmade, artisan brand where the founder's identity is closely linked to customer loyalty.
• At £180,000 revenue, the business may not yet need the scale a merger brings — organic growth lets Sofia test national demand through e-commerce with lower overhead.

Content that could be credited in favour of Option B (merger):
• A merger with a larger distributor gives immediate national shelf space, far outpacing what organic digital growth could achieve in the short term.
• The larger partner may bring warehousing, logistics and marketing resources that Sofia cannot afford alone.

Expected recommendation (Option A is stronger for this context): Sofia's brand identity as a handmade, founder-led product risks being diluted in a merger; converting to Ltd and investing in organic e-commerce growth preserves that identity while managing personal financial risk.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes why a product becomes obsolete?
A) It becomes too expensive to manufacture
B) A better alternative replaces it in the market
C) The government bans it from sale
D) The owner decides to retire
practice_questions.marks: B) A better alternative replaces it in the market [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why changes in technology can create a new business opportunity. Use an example in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks for one developed point.
• 1 mark for identifying a relevant technological change.
• 1 mark for explaining how this creates an opportunity, for example new demand, a new delivery method or a gap in the market.
• 1 mark for a second development, such as a relevant example.

Example answer: The growth of smartphones created demand for mobile services such as food-delivery apps [1]. This gave entrepreneurs a new way to reach customers who wanted restaurant meals at home [1]. Companies such as Deliveroo used that opportunity to build a new market [1].

practice_questions.text: Discuss two reasons why a new business idea might fail in its first year.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks (3 marks per reason).

Mastering (5–6 marks): Two fully developed reasons, each with a clear statement and two logical expansion points showing cause-and-effect reasoning. No context required.

Secure (3–4 marks): Two reasons identified and developed, but one may lack a second expansion point or the logic may not be fully drawn out.

Developing (1–2 marks): One reason identified with limited development, or two reasons stated but neither developed.

Emerging (0 marks): No reasons that are relevant to why a new business fails.

Acceptable reasons include:
• Poor financial management — a business may not have enough cash to pay its bills even if it is making a profit on paper. If customers delay payment while suppliers demand prompt payment, the business can become insolvent and be forced to close.
• Underestimating competition — a new business may enter a market without fully researching rival products or prices. If competitors can undercut the price or offer a better product, customers will switch and the new business will struggle to generate sufficient sales revenue to cover costs.
• Misjudging consumer wants — if the owner has not conducted adequate market research, the product may not meet what customers actually need in terms of price, quality or convenience, leading to low sales.
• Bad timing — launching during an economic downturn reduces consumer spending, making it harder to build a customer base.

practice_questions.text:
Poppy Chen launched a subscription snack box for plant-based diets called ‘Green Pantry Box’ in 2023. She invested £8,000 of personal savings and within six months had 300 paying subscribers, generating £4,500 per month in revenue. However, she found it difficult to pay suppliers on time because most subscribers paid at the end of the month, while her costs were due upfront.

Justify whether or not the risk of starting a business such as Green Pantry Box is worth the potential reward.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 9 marks.

Mastering (8–9 marks): A balanced, well-developed discussion exploring both risk and reward with clear analytical reasoning. The student integrates at least two specific details from the scenario (subscriber numbers, revenue figures, supplier payment timing) into substantive points and reaches a supported view. Arguments are connected, not listed in parallel.

Secure (5–7 marks): Both risk and reward are discussed with some analytical development. At least one specific detail from the scenario is used meaningfully. A conclusion or view is present but may not be fully reasoned.

Developing (2–4 marks): One side (risk or reward) is discussed with some development, or both sides are mentioned but at a surface level without analysis. Scenario details may be named but not used analytically.

Emerging (0–1 mark): Simple or generic observations about risk and reward with little or no reference to the scenario.

Content guidance:
Risks: financial loss (personal savings of £8,000 at stake), business failure, lack of income security, cash-flow pressure (customers paying late while supplier costs are due upfront).
Rewards: 300 paying subscribers and £4,500 monthly revenue suggest strong early demand; profit potential as scale increases; personal satisfaction, independence.
Conclusion: The cash-flow mismatch is the immediate threat despite the promising revenue, suggesting the risk is significant but potentially manageable with better payment terms.

practice_questions.text: Discuss two rewards that motivate entrepreneurs to start a new business.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks (3 marks per reward).

Mastering (5–6 marks): Two fully developed rewards, each with a clear statement and two logical expansion points.

Secure (3–4 marks): Two rewards identified and reasonably developed.

Developing (1–2 marks): One reward identified with limited development, or two rewards stated without development.

Emerging (0 marks): No relevant rewards identified.

Acceptable rewards include:
• Profit — unlike a salary, there is no upper limit on the profit a successful business can generate. As the business grows and costs are managed, profit can increase substantially, providing the entrepreneur with a potentially higher income than employment would offer.
• Independence — being self-employed means the entrepreneur makes their own decisions about working hours, products and strategy. Many entrepreneurs value the freedom to build something that reflects their own vision without answering to an employer.
• Personal satisfaction / challenge — building a business from scratch can be deeply rewarding in a non-financial sense. Seeing an idea become a real product that customers value can provide a sense of achievement that employment often cannot match.

practice_questions.text:
Rajan Patel is considering whether to start a completely original business — a voice-controlled home exercise coach using AI — or adapt an existing business idea by opening a low-cost personal training studio in his local area.

Justify which option Rajan should choose.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 9 marks.

Mastering (8–9 marks): A fully developed recommendation for one option, with well-reasoned analysis of its advantages and acknowledgement of drawbacks. The conclusion is contextualised (references Rajan’s situation, local area context, the nature of both options) and shows clear evaluative judgement. A one-option response that is thoroughly developed can reach this band.

Secure (5–7 marks): A recommendation is made and supported with reasonable analytical points. Some reference to the scenario context. Drawbacks may be acknowledged but not fully weighed against advantages.

Developing (2–4 marks): A recommendation is present but with limited development. Points are made without strong analytical chain, or both options are described in parallel without a clear recommendation.

Emerging (0–1 mark): Little relevant content; no clear recommendation or analysis.

Content guidance:
Adapting the personal training studio: lower risk as the concept is proven; local market is identifiable; start-up investment likely lower; competition exists but is manageable. Drawback: established competitors already in the market.
Original AI exercise coach: higher potential reward if successful; no direct competition yet; however, requires significant technical development, high start-up costs, uncertain consumer demand, and greater risk of failure. Drawback: very high risk for a sole entrepreneur.
Recommendation: the adapted idea (personal training studio) is the more justifiable choice given the lower risk, proven concept, and identifiable local customer base — particularly important for a first-time entrepreneur with limited resources.

practice_questions.text: Define the term ‘unique selling point’ (USP).
practice_questions.marks:
The feature or characteristic that makes a product or business different from, and better than, its competitors. [1 mark]

Also accept: the one thing that distinguishes a business or its product from all rivals in the market.

practice_questions.text: State two ways a business can add value to its products or services.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per correct way, up to 2 marks.
Acceptable answers: convenience / branding / quality / design / unique selling point (USP).
Do not accept vague answers such as “make it better” unless elaborated.

practice_questions.text: Discuss two ways in which an entrepreneur organises resources when starting a business.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks (3 marks per way).

Mastering (5–6 marks): Two fully developed points, each identifying a type of resource and explaining how organising it contributes to the business producing goods/services or adding value. Both points have a clear statement plus two further expansion sentences.

Secure (3–4 marks): Two ways identified and reasonably developed, though one may lack a second expansion.

Developing (1–2 marks): One way explained with limited development, or two ways stated without development.

Emerging (0 marks): No relevant content.

Acceptable content:
• Hiring the right labour — finding employees with the skills the business needs. Without skilled staff, the business cannot produce goods to the required quality, leading to poor customer satisfaction and lost sales.
• Investing in capital — purchasing equipment, machinery or premises needed to produce the product. Without the right tools, productivity will be low and costs per unit will be high, reducing profit.
• Securing raw materials or supplies — negotiating with suppliers to obtain inputs at the right quality and price. If materials are poor quality or too expensive, the business will either fail to add value or be unable to price competitively.

practice_questions.text:
Priya Sharma runs ‘Velvet Root’, a small natural haircare brand in Leeds. She makes all products by hand using ethically sourced plant oils and markets them with the message ‘no chemicals, no compromise’. Her prices are 40% higher than mainstream drugstore brands, but she has built a loyal base of 2,000 online customers who order repeatedly.

Analyse how Velvet Root adds value to its products.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks.

Mastering (5–6 marks): A focused, multi-point analytical response that embeds specific scenario details (ethically sourced oils, 40% price premium, loyal repeat customer base of 2,000, ‘no chemicals’ message) into a coherent argument about how Velvet Root creates value above input costs. The student identifies multiple value-adding methods (likely branding, quality, USP) and explains the mechanism by which each generates customer willingness to pay a premium. A supported conclusion or evaluative comment is present.

Secure (3–4 marks): At least two value-adding methods identified and explained with analytical development. Scenario details are used meaningfully rather than just named.

Developing (1–2 marks): One or two methods identified with limited analytical development. Scenario details are named but not woven into the analysis.

Emerging (0 marks): Generic or barely relevant observations.

Content guidance:
• USP (‘no chemicals, no compromise’ message, ethically sourced inputs) justifies the 40% price premium and differentiates Velvet Root from mass-market rivals.
• Branding (the Velvet Root name, consistent ethical identity) builds loyalty — evidenced by 2,000 repeat customers willing to pay more.
• Quality (handmade, plant oils) adds value by delivering a product perceived as superior, reinforcing the premium price.
• Conclusion: the combination of USP and branding is the primary source of added value; quality underpins both.

practice_questions.text: Discuss two reasons why a business needs to meet customer needs to survive.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks (3 marks per reason).

Mastering (5–6 marks): Two fully developed reasons, each logically connecting unmet customer needs to business failure.

Secure (3–4 marks): Two reasons with reasonable development.

Developing (1–2 marks): One reason explained or two stated without development.

Emerging (0 marks): No relevant content.

Acceptable reasons:
• Generating sales revenue — customers only buy products that meet their needs. If a business fails to provide the right price, quality or convenience, customers will choose a competitor, sales revenue will fall, and the business will be unable to cover its costs, risking failure.
• Business survival — without customers returning, a business cannot grow a loyal base. Word-of-mouth referrals depend on customer satisfaction. A business that consistently fails to meet needs will see declining repeat purchases, making long-term survival increasingly difficult.

practice_questions.text:
‘Branding is the most effective way for a small business to add value to its products.’
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks.

Mastering (10–12 marks): A well-developed, balanced evaluation that considers both the case for branding and the merits of alternative methods (quality, USP, convenience, design), applies analytical reasoning to weigh these, and reaches a genuinely evaluative conclusion that goes beyond summarising earlier points. The conclusion identifies the conditions under which branding is (or is not) the most effective method, referencing business type, customer type or competitive environment.

Secure (7–9 marks): Branding and at least one alternative method are discussed with analytical development. A conclusion is reached but may not fully explain the evaluative reasoning.

Developing (3–6 marks): The statement is discussed with some development, but the analysis is one-sided, the conclusion is a restatement of earlier points, or alternative methods are not considered.

Emerging (0–2 marks): Little relevant content.

Content guidance:
For branding: builds long-term customer loyalty, justifies premium pricing, creates emotional connection beyond the product, difficult for competitors to copy.
Against (alternatives):
• Quality and USP may be more powerful for small businesses that cannot afford major brand marketing.
• Convenience (location, opening hours, delivery speed) may be the primary driver for impulse purchases.
• Design is central for businesses competing on innovation (e.g. tech, fashion).
Conclusion: depends on the type of business — branding is most effective for lifestyle and consumer goods businesses where identity and loyalty matter; less so for price-sensitive commodity businesses where cost and convenience dominate.

before.exam_tip_html: On a 12-mark Evaluate a Statement question, the mark scheme rewards genuine evaluative thinking in the conclusion — not a summary of your previous points. If the statement is “Adding value through branding is the most important role of an entrepreneur”, a Mastering-tier conclusion explains why branding matters more (or less) than other methods of adding value, with a reasoned criterion (e.g. the type of business, the target market, the competitive environment). Phrases like “it depends” without any supporting reasoning earn no evaluation marks. On a 6-mark Analyse question, embedding specific details from the scenario — the product, location, customer type or numerical figures — is what separates a Developing answer from a Secure one. The business name alone does not count as application.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'business objective'.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for a definition that communicates the key idea:
• A specific, measurable target set by a business to help it achieve its broader aims. [1 mark]
(Accept: a target or goal a business works towards, provided it implies it is more specific/measurable than an aim.)

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why a business might change its objective from growing the workforce to reducing it.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• If a business faces falling demand or a recession (1 mark), it may find labour costs are too high relative to revenue (1 mark), making workforce reduction necessary to return to profitability and avoid insolvency (1 mark).
• Other valid reasons: automation replacing labour (1 mark) → technology reduces need for staff (1 mark) → objective shifts from headcount growth to skills investment (1 mark).
[3 marks for a fully contextualised chain of reasoning; 2 marks for a point with some development; 1 mark for a basic point]

practice_questions.text: Discuss why a change in legislation might cause a business to change its aims and objectives.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for the two best-developed points only:

Mastering (5-6 marks): Two fully developed points, each with a clear statement of fact and two logical expansion sentences. Both points are specific to legislation.

Secure (3-4 marks): At least one well-developed point showing how legislation directly alters what a business can or must do, with clear consequences for its objectives.

Developing (1-2 marks): Simple identification of a law affecting a business, with little explanation of why the objective changes.

Emerging (0 marks): No relevant knowledge demonstrated.

Content that could be credited:
• A rise in the National Living Wage increases labour costs for businesses in retail or hospitality — to remain profitable, a business may shift its objective from increasing staffing levels to investing in automation, which completely changes its HR and capital expenditure plans.
• New data protection laws require businesses to allocate resources to compliance — an objective around rapid digital expansion may be paused or scaled back while the business invests in secure data systems to avoid fines and reputational damage.

practice_questions.text: Discuss whether changing market conditions are the most important reason why a business changes its aims and objectives.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A well-balanced discussion that weighs changing market conditions against at least one other trigger (e.g. technology, legislation, performance, internal reasons), with clear chains of analysis and a justified conclusion.

Secure (3–4 marks): Arguments on both sides, with some analytical depth. The conclusion is present but may not be fully reasoned.

Developing (2 marks): Some valid points about market conditions, but the discussion is one-sided or lacks analytical development beyond surface description.

Emerging (1 mark): Basic identification of a reason with no development.

Content that could be credited:
For: Market conditions directly affect demand and revenue — in a recession, a business cannot sustain a growth objective and must pivot to survival; changes in competitor activity can make existing objectives unachievable overnight.
Against: Legislation can be even more immediate — a new law can force a change in objectives regardless of market performance. Technology may be a deeper disruptor over the long term. Internal performance data can trigger a change even when market conditions are favourable.

practice_questions.text:
'Businesses should set long-term aims and objectives and stick to them, regardless of changes in the business environment.'

Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12 marks): A sustained evaluation that examines the argument for consistency in objectives (investor confidence, employee clarity, strategic focus) and the argument for flexibility (adapting to market, legal and technological change). The conclusion introduces new evaluative thinking — for example, arguing that the right approach depends on the rate of change in the business's market.

Secure (7-9 marks): Arguments on both sides, with some evaluative language and a supported conclusion.

Developing (4-6 marks): Points on both sides, but the conclusion is largely a restatement of prior arguments.

Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic description of why aims are important with little or no evaluation.

Content that could be credited:
For the statement: Consistent long-term objectives help attract investors and retain staff who understand the business direction; changing objectives frequently can signal instability.
Against the statement: A business that refuses to update its objectives in the face of new technology, competitor moves or legislation will become uncompetitive. Survival itself may require a complete reset of objectives. Adaptability is a core feature of resilient businesses.

practice_questions.text:
Ridgeline Outdoor Gear is a UK-based retailer selling walking and camping equipment through 12 physical stores. Over the last two years, revenue from in-store sales has fallen by 18% while the market for online outdoor equipment has grown by 35%. The owner, Ben Ashworth, has set a new objective: to close six stores and grow online sales to represent 60% of total revenue within three years.

Analyse whether this change in objectives is likely to benefit Ridgeline Outdoor Gear.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Sustained analysis using specific details from the scenario (18% in-store revenue fall, 35% online market growth, 12 stores, 60% online target, Ben Ashworth's three-year timeline) to evaluate whether the objective change is well-founded. Both benefits and risks are analysed with context-specific reasoning.

Secure (3–4 marks): Clear analysis using some scenario details. Both sides considered but possibly unbalanced or missing one scenario-specific link.

Developing (2 marks): Generic points about why businesses move online or close stores, without close reference to Ridgeline's specific data.

Emerging (1 mark): Basic points with no development.

Content that could be credited:
For: The 35% growth in the online outdoor market aligns with Ben's new objective — redirecting resources from declining physical retail to a growing online channel makes strategic sense. Closing six stores will reduce fixed costs (rent, utilities, staffing), improving short-term profitability while the online transition is funded.
Against: Closing six stores risks losing customers who value in-store advice and product testing — especially important for specialist outdoor gear where touch and fit matter. The 60% online target is ambitious given a starting position of much lower online share; if not achieved, the business will have neither strong store presence nor strong online revenue.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of primary research?
A) Reading a government report on consumer spending
B) Conducting a survey of potential customers at a local market
C) Accessing a published market report from an industry trade body
D) Browsing competitors’ websites for pricing information
practice_questions.marks: B) Conducting a survey of potential customers at a local market [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why a new business should carry out market research before launching its product.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks for one developed point.
• 1 mark for identifying a relevant reason.
• 1 mark for explaining how the reason links to a business outcome.
• 1 mark for a second development, such as the effect on a business with little cash.

Example answer: Market research lets a new business find out what customers need on price and quality before it pays for production [1]. If the product does not meet those needs, sales will be low and the business may not cover its costs [1]. For a new business with small cash reserves, that can lead to insolvency very quickly [1].

practice_questions.text: Discuss two reasons why qualitative research data can be more useful than quantitative data when developing a new product.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks (3 marks per reason).

Mastering (5–6 marks): Two fully developed reasons, each explaining a specific limitation of quantitative data or advantage of qualitative data in the context of product development. Both points have a clear statement and two expansion sentences.

Secure (3–4 marks): Two reasons with reasonable development.

Developing (1–2 marks): One reason explained or two stated without development.

Emerging (0 marks): No relevant content.

Acceptable content:
• Qualitative data reveals why customers behave as they do — a questionnaire can tell a business that 30% of customers dislike a product, but a focus group can explain that the colour, smell or packaging is the specific problem. This insight is directly actionable for product development.
• Qualitative data captures emotional drivers — consumers often buy for reasons that cannot be expressed in a number (aspirational identity, sense of belonging, trust in a brand). Without qualitative research, a business may optimise the wrong variables (e.g. reducing price when the real issue is perceived quality).
• Small sample sizes in qualitative research can still generate rich, specific insights that a large-scale survey might miss because the questions allow for open-ended answers.

practice_questions.text:
Marcus Osei is considering opening a new independent bookshop in a medium-sized market town in the north of England. He has £2,000 to spend on market research. He is deciding between conducting a primary survey of local residents or purchasing a published national market report on the UK independent bookshop sector.

Justify which method of market research Marcus should choose.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 9 marks.

Mastering (8–9 marks): A balanced, analytical discussion that evaluates both methods in the specific context of Marcus's situation (local market town, £2,000 budget, independent bookshop). The student weighs relevance of data against cost, considers the reliability limitations of both methods, and reaches a supported conclusion. Specific scenario details are embedded into the analysis, not just named.

Secure (5–7 marks): Both methods are analysed with some development. At least one specific detail from the scenario is used. A conclusion is reached.

Developing (2–4 marks): One method is discussed with development, or both are mentioned at a surface level. Scenario details may be named but not analysed.

Emerging (0–1 mark): Generic observations with no analytical development or scenario reference.

Content guidance:
Primary survey: highly relevant to Marcus’s specific location and customer base; can ask about book-buying habits, preferences, and willingness to support an independent retailer. Drawback: costly to design and administer on a £2,000 budget; sample may be small.
National market report: cheap and quick; provides data on industry trends, average revenues, competitor landscape. Drawback: national data may not reflect the specific town’s reading culture or demographics; likely to be general rather than hyper-local.
Conclusion: the primary survey is likely more useful because Marcus’s decision is fundamentally local — national trends are secondary to whether his specific community will support an independent bookshop.

practice_questions.text: Discuss two ways in which social media can be used as a market research tool by a small business.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks (3 marks per way).

Mastering (5–6 marks): Two fully developed ways, each explaining the specific mechanism by which social media generates useful research data, with two expansion points per way.

Secure (3–4 marks): Two ways identified and reasonably developed.

Developing (1–2 marks): One way explained or two stated without development.

Emerging (0 marks): No relevant content.

Acceptable ways:
• Running a poll on a social media platform — a business can post a poll asking followers to choose between product options, price points or delivery preferences. This generates quantitative data at near-zero cost and in real time, giving the business quick feedback before committing to a decision.
• Monitoring customer comments and reviews — reading what customers say about existing products (and competitor products) in comments, reviews or direct messages provides qualitative insight into what is working and what needs to change. This form of secondary data collection requires no budget and can highlight trends the business did not anticipate.

practice_questions.text:
Zainab Hussain is planning to launch a new premium skincare range targeting women aged 35–55. She has conducted an online survey of 50 followers on her personal Instagram account and received mostly positive feedback. Her bank manager has told her the research does not appear reliable enough to support a loan application.

Justify whether Zainab should conduct further market research before applying for finance.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 9 marks.

Mastering (8–9 marks): A fully developed recommendation that engages with the specific weaknesses of Zainab’s existing research (self-selecting Instagram audience, small sample size of 50, potential age mismatch) and explains what additional research would address the bank manager’s concerns. The analysis weighs the cost of further research against the risk of loan rejection or product failure. A contextualised, evaluative conclusion justifies the recommendation clearly.

Secure (5–7 marks): A recommendation is made and supported with analysis of the research limitations and the value of additional data. Scenario details are used.

Developing (2–4 marks): A recommendation is present but with limited development. Analysis of reliability issues is superficial.

Emerging (0–1 mark): Little relevant content; no recommendation.

Content guidance:
Case for further research: the Instagram followers are self-selecting and may not represent the target age group (35–55). A sample of 50 is very small for drawing reliable conclusions. The bank manager is unlikely to approve a loan on weak evidence. Better research (face-to-face surveys with the target demographic, focus groups) would strengthen the application and reduce the risk of launching a product with genuinely low demand.
Case against further research: additional research costs time and money Zainab may not have; the positive feedback is a signal, even if imperfect; she could launch on a small scale to test the market first.
Recommendation: yes, further research is justified because the current data has two serious reliability weaknesses (sample size and audience self-selection). Addressing these would both improve the loan application and reduce the business risk of a failed launch.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a tariff?
A) An agreement between countries to remove all trade barriers
B) A tax on imported goods that makes them more expensive
C) A subsidy paid to domestic exporters to lower their prices
D) A restriction on the number of goods a country can export
practice_questions.marks: B) A tax on imported goods that makes them more expensive [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
Fernbrook Textiles imports fabric from a supplier in Vietnam. The cost of one metre of fabric is 12,000 Vietnamese dong (VND). The exchange rate is £1 = 30,000 VND.

Calculate the cost in pounds (£) of one metre of fabric. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Formula: cost in £ = cost in VND ÷ exchange rate
Substitution: 12,000 ÷ 30,000 = £0.40

2 marks for the correct answer of £0.40.
1 mark for the correct method if an arithmetic slip gives the wrong answer.
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one benefit for a UK business of the UK being a member of a trade bloc.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks: 1 mark for the benefit, plus up to 2 marks for developing it.
• Members trade with each other without tariffs (1 mark), so the UK business can sell into those markets at a lower price than firms outside the bloc (1 mark), which helps it win customers and grow its export sales (1 mark).
• Also accept: a much larger customer base; simpler paperwork at the border.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a UK food and drink brand could use e-commerce to compete in an international market.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Two fully developed points showing how e-commerce specifically helps a food/drink brand compete internationally, with chains of reasoning connecting the technology to competitive outcomes.

Secure (3-4 marks): At least one well-developed point using business terminology correctly, showing how e-commerce removes a barrier to international competition.

Developing (1-2 marks): General statement that e-commerce helps businesses sell overseas, with little explanation of how or why.

Emerging (0 marks): No relevant knowledge.

Content that could be credited:
• E-commerce removes the need for expensive retail partnerships or physical distribution networks overseas — a UK craft gin brand can sell directly to customers in Germany or Australia via its own website, dramatically reducing entry costs compared to negotiating shelf space with foreign retailers.
• Online marketplaces (such as Amazon Global) provide ready-made logistics and payment infrastructure, allowing a small food brand to reach millions of customers in multiple countries from a single fulfilment point, making global reach achievable without a large capital investment.

practice_questions.text: Discuss whether globalisation is more of an opportunity than a threat for UK businesses.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A well-balanced discussion with sustained analysis of both opportunities and threats, differentiated by business type, size or sector where relevant. Clear conclusion that adds evaluative thinking about the conditions under which globalisation is more likely to be an opportunity or a threat.

Secure (3–4 marks): Both sides argued with some development. The conclusion is present but may not add new evaluative reasoning.

Developing (2 marks): One side is treated well but the other is underdeveloped or the discussion is generic.

Emerging (1 mark): Only one or two basic points identified.

Content that could be credited:
Opportunities: access to export markets beyond a saturated UK market; cheaper imported raw materials reducing production costs; access to global talent and technology.
Threats: competition from low-cost overseas producers; supply chain vulnerability; exchange rate risk reducing export competitiveness; Brexit-related trade friction for EU-facing businesses.
Conclusion: whether globalisation is more opportunity than threat depends heavily on the business — for a manufacturer competing against cheap imports it is primarily a threat; for a digital service business with a global product it is primarily an opportunity.

practice_questions.text:
Orchard & Rye is a UK artisan cider producer based in Herefordshire with annual revenue of £2.1 million. The owner, James Delacey, is considering expanding internationally. He has two options:

Option A: Enter the French market by adapting the marketing mix and selling through a French drinks distributor.
Option B: Build an e-commerce website to sell directly to consumers across Europe.

Justify which option James should choose.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9 marks): A fully developed recommendation for one option, supported by specific analysis of Orchard & Rye's context (artisan cider, £2.1m revenue, Herefordshire base, European expansion aim). Clear evaluative conclusion explaining why the chosen option fits James's situation better than the alternative.

Secure (5–7 marks): A recommendation with developed analysis using some scenario detail. Considers both options but may not evaluate them in equal depth.

Developing (3–4 marks): A preference is stated with some relevant points, but analysis is largely generic.

Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic preference stated with minimal development.

Content that could be credited for Option A (distributor):
• A French distributor already has relationships with retailers and restaurants — crucial in France where on-trade (bars, restaurants) accounts for a large share of premium drinks sales.
• The distributor manages language, regulation and customs complexity, reducing the burden on a small Herefordshire operation.
• Risk: James loses some control over pricing and branding, which matters for an artisan product where premium positioning is the core value.

Content that could be credited for Option B (e-commerce):
• Lower set-up cost and full control over branding and customer relationships.
• Risk: international shipping of fragile glass bottles is expensive; regulatory compliance for food/drink varies by country; building European brand awareness without a distributor's network takes time.

Expected recommendation: Option A is stronger for a £2.1m artisan producer — the distributor route provides immediate market access without the logistics and regulatory burden that would stretch a small team.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'pressure group'.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for a definition that communicates the key idea:
• An organised group of people who seek to influence the decisions of businesses or governments to advance a particular cause. [1 mark]
(Accept any definition that identifies: organised, aims to influence, a specific cause.)

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which a pressure group could affect a food manufacturer's marketing mix.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• A pressure group could campaign against the use of a harmful ingredient, such as palm oil (1 mark). This may force the manufacturer to reformulate the product (1 mark), which could increase production costs and lead to a higher selling price or reduced profit margin (1 mark).
• Alternative routes: pressure on promotion (forced to reword health claims), place (retailers refuse to stock), product (redesign packaging to remove single-use plastic).
[3 marks for a fully developed chain; 2 for a clear point with development; 1 for a basic point]

practice_questions.text: Discuss why acting ethically might create a trade-off for a business.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for the two best-developed points only:

Mastering (5-6 marks): Two fully developed points, each with a clear statement and two logical expansion sentences showing how the ethical action creates a specific cost or compromise for the business.

Secure (3-4 marks): At least one well-developed point that clearly links an ethical decision to a business cost or strategic impact.

Developing (1-2 marks): A simple identification of a trade-off with limited explanation.

Emerging (0 marks): No relevant business knowledge.

Content that could be credited:
• Ethical sourcing requires a business to pay higher prices for fairly traded raw materials or components — this raises cost of sales, which either squeezes profit margins or forces the business to raise its selling price, risking a loss of price-sensitive customers to less ethical rivals.
• Paying workers a living wage above the legal minimum increases the business’s wage bill — the business must either accept lower profit or cut costs elsewhere (e.g. reduce staffing levels), which may reduce the quality or speed of its service and affect customer satisfaction.

practice_questions.text:
Vantage Sports Co. makes sports trainers sold in high-street stores across the UK. Annual revenue is £6.8 million. A pressure group recently published evidence that one of Vantage's overseas manufacturers uses excessive working hours and pays below the local minimum wage. The campaign has reached 200,000 social media users in one week.

Analyse the potential impact of this pressure group campaign on Vantage Sports Co.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Sustained analysis using specific scenario details (£6.8m revenue, high-street retail, 200,000 social media users, overseas manufacturing) to evaluate the short- and long-term impact on Vantage. Both the reputational and financial consequences explored with chains of reasoning linked to Vantage’s specific context.

Secure (3–4 marks): Clear analysis using at least two scenario-specific details. Both immediate and longer-term impacts considered but possibly with less depth.

Developing (2 marks): Some valid points about pressure group impact on a business, but largely generic and not closely tied to Vantage’s context.

Emerging (1 mark): Basic identification of an impact with no development.

Content that could be credited:
• The 200,000 social media reach creates rapid brand damage — for a high-street sports brand, where consumers directly associate the product with the brand’s values, this could reduce foot traffic in stores and trigger retailer pressure to audit or drop the line.
• Vantage faces a short-term financial impact if retailers demand immediate changes — switching manufacturer or enforcing new supplier standards costs time and money; if the £6.8m revenue falls even 5%, the resulting shortfall could be difficult for a relatively small business to absorb.
• Responding proactively — publishing a supplier audit and committing to ethical standards — can turn the crisis into a brand-building opportunity, though this requires investment in supply chain management that was not previously in the budget.

practice_questions.text:
'Businesses should always prioritise ethical and environmental considerations over profitability.'

Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12 marks): A sustained evaluation that examines the argument for prioritising ethics and environment (reputation, loyalty, regulatory risk, long-term sustainability) and the argument for prioritising profitability (without profit a business cannot survive, invest or employ people). The conclusion introduces a new evaluative criterion — for example, whether the trade-off matters more in consumer-facing markets than in B2B ones, or whether it depends on the time horizon.

Secure (7-9 marks): Both sides argued with development and some evaluative language. A supported conclusion present.

Developing (4-6 marks): Some points on both sides but the conclusion is largely a restatement of prior arguments.

Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic description of why ethics matter or why profit matters, with little evaluation.

Content that could be credited:
For: Consumers increasingly favour ethical brands, meaning ethics can directly support long-term profit through premium pricing and loyalty. Environmental investment avoids future regulatory penalties. Workers in ethical workplaces are more motivated and productive.
Against: A business that consistently sacrifices profit for ethics may not be viable in the long term — without profit it cannot invest, grow or employ people. In highly competitive, price-driven markets, ethical premium pricing risks losing customers. Small businesses in particular may lack the margins to absorb ethical costs that larger competitors can spread over higher volumes.
Conclusion example: The statement goes too far — in the short term, a business must be profitable enough to survive; however, businesses that consistently ignore ethical and environmental concerns face growing reputational and regulatory risk that ultimately threatens their long-term profitability more than the cost of acting ethically would have done.

practice_questions.text:
Pemberton Farms is a family-owned dairy business in Somerset with annual revenue of £1.4 million. Growing consumer awareness of environmental issues is affecting the business. The owner, Rachel Pemberton, is considering two options:

Option A: Invest £120,000 in solar panels and reduce the business’s carbon footprint, marketing the farm as a sustainable, ethical producer.
Option B: Focus entirely on cutting costs and competing on price to defend market share against lower-cost imported dairy products.

Justify which option Rachel should choose.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9 marks): A fully developed recommendation for one option, supported by specific analysis of Pemberton Farms’ context (family-owned, Somerset, £1.4m revenue, dairy sector, consumer environmental awareness trend, £120,000 investment). Clear evaluative conclusion that acknowledges the rejected option’s appeal but explains why the chosen option better suits this business.

Secure (5–7 marks): A clear recommendation with developed analysis using some scenario detail. Both options considered.

Developing (3–4 marks): A preference stated with some relevant points but largely generic.

Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic preference with minimal development.

Content that could be credited for Option A (sustainability investment):
• Consumer awareness of environmental issues is growing — an ethical brand identity can command premium pricing in the premium dairy segment, protecting margins rather than eroding them through a price war.
• A family farm in Somerset has the provenance story that consumers increasingly associate with sustainable food; the solar investment makes that story credible and auditable.
• Risk: £120,000 is a significant outlay relative to £1.4m revenue; payback depends on how quickly premium pricing offsets the investment.

Content that could be credited for Option B (cut costs / compete on price):
• Cutting costs is immediately actionable and does not require capital investment.
• Risk: competing on price against large importers is a race to the bottom for a small family farm that cannot match their scale economies.

Expected recommendation: Option A is stronger — Pemberton Farms cannot win a price war against industrial importers, but it can differentiate on provenance and sustainability, which aligns with growing consumer values and protects margins.

practice_questions.text: Define the term ‘market segmentation’.
practice_questions.marks:
Dividing a market into distinct groups of customers who share similar characteristics. [1 mark]

Also accept: splitting potential customers into smaller groups based on shared needs or characteristics such as age, income, location or lifestyle.

practice_questions.text: State two ways a business could segment its market.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per correct segmentation method, up to 2 marks.
Acceptable answers: location / demographics / lifestyle / income / age.
Do not accept vague answers such as “by type of customer” unless a specific variable is identified.

practice_questions.text:
Nimra Ashraf is planning to open a premium nail salon targeting professional women aged 25–45 in central Birmingham. She has drawn a market map comparing existing nail salons in the area on price (low to high) and quality of service (low to high).

Analyse how market mapping could help Nimra decide where to position her business.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks.

Mastering (5–6 marks): A well-developed analytical response that uses the specific context (premium nail salon, professional women 25–45, Birmingham city centre, price vs quality axes) to explain how the market map would reveal competitor positions and an unoccupied space. The student analyses how Nimra would use this information to set her price and quality positioning, and acknowledges at least one limitation of the map in context.

Secure (3–4 marks): The benefit of market mapping is explained with some analytical development. At least one specific detail from the scenario is used meaningfully. A limitation may be noted.

Developing (1–2 marks): A basic explanation of market mapping with little connection to Nimra’s specific situation.

Emerging (0 marks): No relevant content.

Content guidance:
• The map would show if the premium / high-quality quadrant is already crowded with competitors or has space for a new entrant.
• If competitors cluster in the low-price / lower-quality segment, a gap exists for a premium service — directly aligning with Nimra’s intended positioning.
• Limitation: the map only captures two variables; it cannot show the loyalty of existing customers, the volume of demand in each segment, or whether Birmingham’s professional women actively want a new premium option.

practice_questions.text:
Devraj Singh runs ‘Copper & Clay’, a handmade jewellery business based in Edinburgh. He currently targets all adult women equally through a general social media presence, but sales have plateaued. His market research shows that 70% of his best-selling items appeal to women aged 30–55 with mid-to-high incomes who value ethically sourced materials.

Analyse how Devraj could use market segmentation to improve the performance of Copper & Clay.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks.

Mastering (5–6 marks): A focused, multi-point analytical response that embeds specific scenario details (plateaued sales, 70% of best sellers matching a demographic profile, Edinburgh, ethical sourcing) into a coherent argument about how targeted segmentation would improve marketing efficiency and revenue. The student identifies the most relevant segmentation variables for this business (demographics: age 30–55; income: mid-to-high; lifestyle: values ethical sourcing), analyses the mechanism by which focusing on these segments would improve performance, and reaches a supported evaluative conclusion.

Secure (3–4 marks): Two or more segmentation approaches are analysed with development. Specific scenario details are used. A conclusion is present.

Developing (1–2 marks): Segmentation is discussed but mostly at a surface level. Scenario details may be named but not embedded in analysis.

Emerging (0 marks): Generic or barely relevant observations.

Content guidance:
• Demographic segmentation (30–55, mid-to-high income) would allow Devraj to direct his social media budget and messaging to this group specifically, reducing wasted spend on audiences unlikely to buy.
• Lifestyle segmentation (ethical sourcing as a value) would sharpen the USP — marketing the ethical story prominently would resonate with this segment and justify the premium price.
• Combining demographic and lifestyle segmentation (e.g. targeting via Instagram ads to women aged 35–50 in Scotland interested in sustainable fashion) would be more precise than a general social media presence.
• Risk: over-segmenting could exclude occasional buyers from other groups; the market may be smaller than the current broad approach suggests.

practice_questions.text: Discuss two reasons why identifying customer segments is important for a new small business.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks (3 marks per reason).

Mastering (5–6 marks): Two fully developed reasons, each explaining the mechanism by which segmentation benefits a new small business, with two expansion sentences per reason.

Secure (3–4 marks): Two reasons with reasonable development.

Developing (1–2 marks): One reason explained or two stated without development.

Emerging (0 marks): No relevant content.

Acceptable reasons:
• More efficient use of a limited marketing budget — a new small business rarely has the resources to advertise broadly. By targeting a specific segment, it can focus spending on the channels and messages most likely to convert. This reduces wasted spend and maximises the return on every marketing pound.
• Better product fit and higher customer satisfaction — designing a product for a specific segment (e.g. high-income consumers who value sustainability) means the product can be tailored precisely to that group’s needs. Customers whose needs are met accurately are more likely to return and recommend the business, helping to build a loyal customer base quickly.

practice_questions.text:
Saffron Leigh is launching a new plant-based ready meal brand in the UK. She has two options: target the broad ‘health-conscious adult’ segment, or focus specifically on the ‘vegan families with children’ niche segment.

Justify which segmentation approach Saffron should choose for the launch of her brand.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 9 marks.

Mastering (8–9 marks): A fully developed recommendation for one approach, with well-reasoned analysis of its advantages and an honest acknowledgement of its drawbacks in the specific context of a new plant-based brand. The conclusion is evaluative — it explains the conditions under which this recommendation holds, rather than restating prior points. A one-option focus that is thoroughly developed can reach this band.

Secure (5–7 marks): A recommendation is made with analytical support. Some reference to the scenario. Drawbacks acknowledged.

Developing (2–4 marks): A recommendation is present but with limited analytical development or no clear weighing of advantages against disadvantages.

Emerging (0–1 mark): Little relevant content; no clear recommendation.

Content guidance:
Broad ‘health-conscious adult’ segment: larger addressable market, more revenue potential at scale, wider distribution opportunities. Drawback: highly competitive (Quorn, Beyond Meat, etc. already occupying this space), harder to differentiate, marketing message may be diluted.
Vegan families niche: smaller but under-served segment; clearer differentiation (family-friendly portions, child-appropriate flavours, ethical parenting angle); word-of-mouth potential within close-knit community; easier to build a distinctive brand identity. Drawback: smaller total market, so revenue ceiling may be lower initially.
Recommendation: the niche segment is the stronger launch choice because it offers clear differentiation in a crowded market — a new brand cannot compete on volume with established players, but it can build a loyal community around a specific identity. Scale-up is possible once the brand is established.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes the maturity phase of the product life cycle?
A) Sales are rising rapidly and the business is reinvesting profits into awareness campaigns
B) Sales have peaked and competition is fierce, often pushing prices down
C) The product has just launched and costs exceed revenue
D) Sales are falling and the business must decide whether to withdraw the product
practice_questions.marks: B) Sales have peaked and competition is fierce, often pushing prices down [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline one element of the design mix.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for naming an element of the design mix, plus 1 mark for a linked point about it.
• Function (1 mark) — the product has to do its job well, or customers will not buy it again (1 mark).
• Also accept: aesthetics (how it looks and feels) or cost (what it takes to make).
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Dune & Stone is a small homeware brand based in Norwich. It has just launched a new range of handmade ceramic mugs. Explain one reason why Dune & Stone might use an extension strategy in the future.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks. Students should give a reason for using an extension strategy and develop the point in context:
• Dune & Stone may use an extension strategy when mug sales begin to decline (1 mark) because without action, revenue and profit will fall as customers switch to newer or cheaper alternatives (1 mark), leaving the business with unsold stock and wasted production capacity (1 mark).
• Award 1 mark for a relevant reason, 1 mark for development of that reason, and 1 mark for a contextual link to the scenario (homeware / small brand / customer loyalty).

practice_questions.text: Discuss how the design mix can help a business differentiate its product.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks per point (statement + two expansions), maximum 6 marks. No case-study context is required.

Point 1 — Aesthetics:
A business can differentiate by prioritising aesthetics (1), making the product look and feel more appealing than rivals (1), which can justify a price premium and attract customers who are willing to pay more for an attractive design (1).

Point 2 — Function:
A business can differentiate through superior function (1), engineering the product to perform better or last longer than competitors’ versions (1), which builds customer loyalty and positive word-of-mouth that reduces future marketing costs (1).

[Only the best two points are marked. A third point earns no credit.]

practice_questions.text:
Revel Print Co. is a mid-sized greeting card company based in Edinburgh. It sells 600,000 cards per year at an average price of £3.50. The market for physical greeting cards has been in steady decline for three years. A rival company has just launched a digital card subscription service. Revel Print’s managing director is considering an extension strategy to revive sales.

Analyse how the product life cycle phase that Revel Print Co. is currently in might affect its marketing decisions.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): The student identifies Revel Print as being in the decline phase and develops two or more well-connected analytical points that integrate specific contextual details (the 600,000 cards, £3.50 price, three-year decline, digital rival). Analysis shows how the decline phase affects both the marketing budget decision and the type of promotion strategy likely to succeed. A clear evaluative thread connects phase to decision.

Secure (3–4 marks): The student correctly identifies the decline phase and makes at least one analytical point linking the phase to a specific marketing decision. Context from the scenario is used but may not be embedded in every paragraph.

Developing (2 marks): The student describes characteristics of the decline phase correctly but the link to marketing decisions is general rather than analytical. Limited use of the numerical or business-specific details in the source.

Emerging (1 mark): Basic recall of a product life cycle phase or a generic statement about marketing with little or no contextual application.

practice_questions.text:
Revel Print Co. is considering two options to revive sales:
Option A: Redesign the cards using premium recycled materials and raise the average price to £5.00, targeting the premium gift market.
Option B: Partner with a national supermarket chain to reduce the price to £1.99 and significantly increase volume.

Justify which option you would recommend to Revel Print Co.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9 marks): A clear recommendation is made and fully justified using specific details from the context (current price of £3.50, 600,000 volume, three-year decline). The student develops a coherent case for the chosen option, addresses likely drawbacks and explains why those drawbacks are manageable. The conclusion adds a new evaluative point rather than summarising earlier arguments.

Secure (5–7 marks): A recommendation is made with developed analytical reasoning using some contextual detail. One or more potential drawbacks of the chosen option are acknowledged. The conclusion is present but may restate earlier points.

Developing (3–4 marks): A recommendation is made with some reasoning, but analysis is general and context from the source is used only superficially. The student may address both options in parallel without reaching a clear justified conclusion.

Emerging (1–2 marks): A preference is stated with limited or no reasoning. No meaningful use of the contextual details provided.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a dimension on which businesses typically assess competitor strengths and weaknesses?
A) Staff turnover rate
B) Customer service
C) Number of shareholders
D) Corporation tax rate
practice_questions.marks: B) Customer service [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
Outline one way in which an understanding of the competitive environment can help a small business owner make better decisions.
The business is a new independent florist opening in a town that already has two florists.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for one outlined point: 1 mark for a relevant factor, 1 mark for a linked development placed in context.

Acceptable points include:
• Knowing a rival's price range lets the new florist set a competitive price without starting a damaging price war.
• Spotting that the existing florists have narrow ranges (for example, no wedding flowers) lets the new florist specialise and serve an underserved group.
• Spotting a rival's weak customer service (for example, slow delivery) lets the new florist compete on same-day delivery as a USP.

practice_questions.text: Discuss two ways in which the competitive environment can affect a small business's pricing decisions.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks (3 per way). The best two developed points only are marked.

Point 1 — Competitive pricing pressure:
A business may have to reduce its prices when rivals undercut it to avoid losing customers. This is especially true where the product is similar and customers can easily switch, so the business must match the market rate or risk losing sales and revenue.

Point 2 — Premium pricing opportunity:
If competitors offer low-quality products, a business can charge more by emphasising superior quality. Customers willing to pay a premium represent a segment that competitors with a low-cost strategy cannot easily serve.

Point 3 (if offered instead) — Price matching to retain market share:
When a major competitor cuts prices significantly, a business may match the cut in the short term to protect its customer base, even at the cost of lower profit margins, until the competitive pressure eases.

Each way: 1 mark for a basic statement of fact; +1 for a logical development; +1 for a second development step that further extends the point. No context is given in Discuss questions.

practice_questions.text:
Harbour Lane Bikes is a small independent bicycle shop in a coastal town. It sells a range of road, mountain and children's bikes. A large national cycling retailer recently opened a store nearby, offering lower prices, a wider product range and an in-store café. Harbour Lane's owner, Priya, is considering how to respond.

Analyse how understanding the competitive environment might help Priya make decisions about the future of Harbour Lane Bikes.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Detailed, contextualised analysis of at least two competitive dimensions (e.g. product range and customer service) with explicit reference to Harbour Lane's coastal location, customer base, or product mix. Shows how a specific competitive weakness of the rival (e.g. it is a national chain with less personal service) creates an opportunity for Priya. Draws a reasoned conclusion about the most viable response given the business's small-business context.

Secure (3–4 marks): Analysis of at least two dimensions with some contextual reference. May identify a competitive response but reasoning is partially developed. The case-study context is used but not deeply embedded throughout.

Developing (2 marks): Describes one or two competitive dimensions with limited analysis. Some attempt to apply to Harbour Lane but relies mainly on general points. Limited development of consequences.

Emerging (1 mark): Basic identification of competitive factors with little or no application to the scenario.

practice_questions.text: State two ways a small business can gather information about a competitor's strengths and weaknesses.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per correct method, up to 2 marks. Accept any two of the following:
• Visit or observe the competitor's premises [1]
• Purchase the competitor's products and evaluate them [1]
• Read online customer reviews of the competitor [1]
• Speak to customers who have used the competitor [1]
• Analyse the competitor's website or social media [1]
• Consult market reports or trade publications [1]

practice_questions.text:
Thornfield Provisions is a small deli and grocery shop in a market town. The owner, Marcus, is deciding between two options:

Option A: Focus entirely on locally sourced, premium products and raise prices by 10%.
Option B: Broaden the product range to include everyday grocery staples and hold current prices.

A large supermarket has recently opened on the edge of town. Justify which option Marcus should choose.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9 marks): A fully developed case for one option, acknowledging the main drawback of that option and explaining why it is outweighed in this specific context. The recommendation is clearly justified using competitive environment logic (e.g. the supermarket will always beat Thornfield on price and everyday range, so differentiation through premium local provenance is the only sustainable strategy). Conclusion adds new evaluative insight rather than merely summarising.

Secure (5–7 marks): A developed argument for one or both options with some context. Reasoning is clear but the conclusion may not add new evaluative thinking or may not fully address the competitive threat from the supermarket.

Developing (2–4 marks): Some relevant points about each option but largely descriptive. Limited connection to the competitive environment or the specific deli context.

Emerging (0–1 mark): Basic identification of features of each option with little analysis or justification.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'revenue'.
practice_questions.marks: Revenue is the total money received by a business from selling its products or services, calculated as price multiplied by quantity sold. [1 mark — must include the idea of price × quantity or total income from sales]

practice_questions.text:
A business sells 500 units at a price of £8 each. Its fixed costs are £1,800 and its variable costs are £3 per unit.

Calculate the business's total costs.
practice_questions.marks:
Formula: Total costs = Total fixed costs + Total variable costs
Total variable costs = £3 × 500 = £1,500
Total costs = £1,800 + £1,500 = £3,300 [2 marks for correct final answer of £3,300; allow 1 mark if correct method shown but arithmetic error]

practice_questions.text:
A business borrows £15,000 and repays a total of £18,750 over three years.

Calculate the total interest paid as a percentage of the amount borrowed. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Formula: Interest (%) = ((Total repayment − Amount borrowed) ÷ Amount borrowed) × 100
Substitution: ((18,750 − 15,000) ÷ 15,000) × 100
= (3,750 ÷ 15,000) × 100
= 25%
[3 marks: 1 mark for identifying the interest amount (£3,750); 1 mark for correct division (÷ 15,000); 1 mark for correct final answer of 25%. Allow follow-through from earlier arithmetic errors if method is correct.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss two reasons why a small business owner might have non-financial aims for their business.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks; only the best two developed points count.

Point 1 — Personal satisfaction/independence:
A business owner may aim for independence and control because they want to make their own decisions rather than following orders from an employer. This non-financial aim reflects a desire for autonomy — the owner values freedom over maximising their salary.

Point 2 — Social objectives:
An owner may aim to benefit the community or environment, for example by using local suppliers or reducing packaging waste. Achieving this social objective may actually reduce profit, but the owner values the social impact of their business more than additional financial return.

Point 3 (if offered) — Personal challenge:
Some entrepreneurs start a business to prove to themselves (and others) that a concept can work. The challenge of building something from scratch is motivating in itself, even if financial rewards are limited in the short term.

1 mark per basic statement of fact; +1 for logical development; +1 for a further step that extends the point. No context is given in Discuss questions.

practice_questions.text:
Saltwick Press is a small independent bookshop in a seaside town. The owner, Fiona, set it up three years ago. In year one, her only aim was to survive. Now that the business is profitable, she is considering whether to focus on maximising profit or to expand her social media presence and run community reading events that may not directly increase sales.

Justify whether or not Fiona should change her business objectives now that Saltwick Press is established.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9 marks): Extended, analytical discussion of financial and non-financial objectives with clear reasoning about why a business's objectives evolve over time. May bring in the bookshop context (seasonal trade, community ties, independent vs online retail competition). Reaches a developed judgement about which direction is more appropriate for this type of business, backed by reasoning.

Secure (5–7 marks): Discusses both financial and non-financial objectives with some developed reasoning. May not fully contextualise within the bookshop scenario but reasoning about the trade-off between profit and social objectives is present.

Developing (3–4 marks): Identifies financial and non-financial aims with basic development. Limited connection to how or why objectives change as a business matures.

Emerging (1–2 marks): Lists types of aims with little or no analysis of the trade-off or context.

practice_questions.text:
Brightside Fitness is a start-up gym with 120 members. It charges £35 per month. Monthly fixed costs are £2,800. Variable costs are £5 per member per month.

Calculate Brightside Fitness's monthly profit.
practice_questions.marks:
Formula: Profit = Revenue − Total costs
Revenue = £35 × 120 = £4,200
Total variable costs = £5 × 120 = £600
Total costs = £2,800 + £600 = £3,400
Profit = £4,200 − £3,400 = £800
[3 marks: 1 mark for correct revenue (£4,200); 1 mark for correct total costs (£3,400); 1 mark for correct profit figure (£800). Allow follow-through on arithmetic errors if method is clear.]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'penetration pricing'.
practice_questions.marks: Launching a product at a low price to gain market share quickly before raising the price later. [1 mark — accept any accurate definition that captures the low-launch-price and market-share objective]

practice_questions.text:
Harbour & Bloom is a small artisan candle business in Truro. It sells a standard candle for £12.00. Its new premium candle sells for £20.00.

Calculate the percentage increase in price from the standard candle to the premium candle. Give your answer to one decimal place.
practice_questions.marks:
Formula: percentage change = (change in price ÷ original price) × 100
Substitution: (£20.00 − £12.00) ÷ £12.00 × 100 = 66.7%

2 marks for the correct answer of 66.7%.
1 mark for the correct method if an arithmetic slip gives the wrong answer.
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Harbour & Bloom is considering two promotional strategies: sponsoring a local craft fair (£500 cost) or running targeted advertising on social media (£500 budget). Explain one benefit of using targeted online advertising for Harbour & Bloom.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks for a benefit with development and context:
• Targeted online advertising allows Harbour & Bloom to reach users who have already shown interest in gifts or candles (1 mark), meaning the £500 budget is spent only on people likely to buy (1 mark), which improves the return on promotion spend compared with sponsoring a general craft fair where many visitors may have no interest in candles (1 mark).
[1 mark for a relevant benefit, 1 mark for development, 1 mark for a contextual link to the scenario]

practice_questions.text:
Analyse how the stage of the product life cycle can influence a business's choice of pricing strategy.

Paragon Robotics Ltd has launched an innovative domestic cleaning robot priced at £899. It is the only product of its type currently on the market.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Identifies that Paragon Robotics is in the introduction phase and correctly connects this to a skimming strategy with at least two well-developed analytical points.
